balance-sheet.title: Balance sheet
balance-sheet.concept: The balance sheet is a snapshot of Adidas on 31 December. Assets show what the group owns: stores, warehouses, the brand, €5.8bn of sneakers in stock, invoices retailers have not paid yet, and cash. Liabilities show who financed it all: shareholders (equity), banks and bondholders (financial debts, which cost interest) and the Asian factories Adidas pays after 90 days (operating debt, free if paid on time). Both columns are always equal. To judge financial health, switch to the economic view: capital employed (fixed assets + WCR) financed by equity and net debt. Gross debt is not what matters; net debt is. For solvency, look at the stable resources / capital employed ratio, and distrust liquidity ratios.

lab.title: Adidas's 2025 balance sheet, two readings
lab.goal: Switch between the accounting and the economic balance sheet: watch the WCR and the net debt appear, compare the stable resources / capital employed ratio with the course thresholds, then test yourself with the liquidity and solvency MCQ.

pdfExample.original: Exercise 1 "Balance sheet" (accounting then economic) and the Europcar solvency exercise.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas's consolidated balance sheet at 31/12/2025, reclassified line by line into the course template.

income-statement.title: Income statement
income-statement.concept: The income statement tells the story of Adidas's year: wealth created (€24.8bn of footwear, apparel and accessories sold in 2025) minus wealth destroyed (products made in Asia, salaries, marketing, store rents, depreciation). It flows down like a waterfall: EBITDA, then EBIT (operating result, €2.06bn), the financial result (the cost of debt), tax, and finally the net result (€1.39bn). Classic trap: result ≠ cash. Depreciating a flagship store is a calculated expense, no cash leaves. A pair sold to a retailer who pays in 60 days is income, but not yet a single euro in the bank. The result is partly virtual; cash is real. Finally, the break-even point: with high fixed costs (stores, sponsorship), a small drop in sales can sink the result.

lab.title: From turnover to net result
lab.goal: Move sales, gross margin, operating expenses, depreciation, financial result and tax rate: the waterfall recalculates, the break-even point moves, and the result / cash gap of the pop-up store appears.

pdfExample.original: Pizza Food Truck (result ≠ cash, pessimistic scenario with an overdraft) and the Fever Tech exercise (by-nature and by-function formats).
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas Originals pop-up store (same mechanics, amounts ×10) and an Adidas running-shoe assembly workshop (volumes ×10, prices ÷10: same totals as the course answer).

wcr.title: Working Capital Requirement
wcr.concept: Adidas pays its factories in Asia after about 90 days. But a pair of Ultraboost spends almost six months in stock (ship, warehouse, shelf), then the retailer pays some forty days after delivery. Between the cash paid to the factory and the cash collected on the sale, there is a gap to finance permanently: the Working Capital Requirement (WCR). Each invoice turns over quickly, but their total stays stable: a permanent need, to be financed by stable resources, like a warehouse. Three "nice" reflexes make it grow: building up stock, giving customers more time, paying suppliers faster. And strong growth inflates the WCR: without financing, net cash collapses. You can die in excellent health.

lab.title: WCR & net cash simulator
lab.goal: Set Adidas's customer and supplier payment terms and its storage time, then sales growth: WCR, capital employed and net cash (stable resources − capital employed) update in real time.

pdfExample.original: The "twin companies" A (negative WCR) and B (unfinanced growth, overdraft), and American Airlines (WCR of −$13,457m).
pdfExample.adidas: adidas.com (online sales paid upfront: negative WCR) versus a wholesale subsidiary (retailers paying on credit: positive WCR that doubles with sales).

profitability.title: ROCE & ROE
profitability.concept: Adidas puts about €10.8bn of capital employed to work: stores, warehouses, brand, inventory. ROCE measures what this capital earns after tax, however it is financed: NOPAT / capital employed. It splits into margin × rotation: Adidas lives mainly on its margin (premium brand), Carrefour on how fast its shelves turn. ROE measures the return for shareholders: net profit / equity. The bridge between them is the leverage effect: as long as ROCE exceeds the after-tax cost of debt (kD), every euro borrowed boosts ROE. But if sales fall and ROCE drops below kD, leverage works in reverse and amplifies the fall. And the more Adidas borrows, the higher the rate lenders demand.

lab.title: Leverage simulator
lab.goal: Change the net debt (D), the equity (E), the operating result and the cost of debt: ROCE and ROE recalculate instantly. Push ROCE below kD to see leverage turn against you.

pdfExample.original: 2019 ROCE of Apple (29%), LVMH (18%), Carrefour (7%) and Volkswagen (2%); proof of the leverage formula.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas's 2025 ROCE and ROE computed from its economic balance sheet and its EBIT.

wacc.title: WACC
wacc.concept: To finance its capital employed, Adidas relies on two kinds of investors. Shareholders require kE: they bear the most risk, with no planned repayment. Lenders require kD, which is cheaper, and further reduced by the tax saving on interest. The WACC is their weighted average: the minimum return each euro invested must deliver. It is the bar to clear. ROCE > WACC: Adidas creates value, and the market value of its equity exceeds its book value (goodwill). ROCE < WACC: value destruction, even with a positive net profit. The temptation: replace equity with "cheaper" debt. It does not work: risk rises, so do kD and kE. The WACC depends on the risk of the business, not on how you slice the pizza.

lab.title: WACC and value creation
lab.goal: Set kE, the pre-tax borrowing rate, the tax rate and the equity / net debt split: the WACC recalculates. Then vary the NOPAT to replay the course cases A, B and C (neutral, goodwill, badwill).

pdfExample.original: Simplified company: fixed assets 65 + WCR 35 = equity 60 + net debt 40, kE 14%, kD 4%, WACC 10%, cases A/B/C.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas simplified to €10bn of capital employed (6.5 + 3.5 = 6 + 4), with the same rates: NOPAT of €1.0bn, €1.7bn and €0.6bn.

npv-irr.title: NPV & IRR
npv-irr.concept: Adidas is considering €100m of R&D on a new sole, expected to bring in €25m of cash a year for 5 years. €125m collected for €100m spent: a good deal? Not so fast. A euro in 5 years is not worth a euro today (risk, inflation, opportunity cost). So each free cash flow is discounted at the return investors require, usually the WACC. The sum, minus the initial investment, is the NPV: positive, the project creates value; negative, stop. At 10%, the sole shows an NPV of −€5m; at 5%, +€8m. The IRR is the rate that brings the NPV to zero, here 8%: easy to read, but misleading when choosing between mutually exclusive projects. To decide, the NPV is what counts.

lab.title: Investment lab
lab.goal: Pick an Adidas project (R&D sole, flagship store, mutually exclusive projects) or enter your own cash flows, then vary the discount rate: NPV, IRR and payback recalculate, and the NPV = f(rate) curve shows where it crosses zero.

pdfExample.original: A €100k machine earning €25k a year for 5 years; exercise 3 (€20m plant extension); mutually exclusive projects of exercise 1.
pdfExample.adidas: €100m R&D on a sole; €20m new flagship store; choosing between a Shanghai flagship and a padel apparel line.

cash-flow.title: Cash flow statement
cash-flow.concept: "Cash is king." The result is partly virtual; cash is real, and when it runs out, it's death. The cash flow statement explains how Adidas's cash changed through three flows. Cash flows from operations (CFO): EBITDA, minus tax, minus the WCR increase. Cash flows from investments (CFI): factories, warehouses and software bought, minus disposals. Their sum is the free cash flow (FCFF), the cash Adidas can freely use. Then come cash flows from financing (CFF): loans, repayments, interest, dividends. In 2025, Adidas posted €3.1bn of EBITDA but only €0.75bn of CFO: inventories and receivables swallowed more than €2bn. After €0.4bn of investments and €1.1bn paid to lenders and shareholders, its cash shrank by €838m.

lab.title: From EBITDA to free cash flow
lab.goal: Start from Adidas's 2025 EBITDA, play with customer terms, storage time, supplier terms and CAPEX (a new factory?): the waterfall down to FCFF recalculates live. Complete the missions, then dissect the real 2025 cash flow statement with the questions of the ENGIE exercise.

pdfExample.original: ENGIE 2015 exercise: negative net result but more than €10bn of operating cash flows; uses of cash and split of the FCFF among capital providers.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas's 2025 consolidated cash flow statement (annual report), regrouped into the course template: the opposite of ENGIE, a good result but a CFO crushed by the WCR.

solvency.title: Solvency
solvency.concept: Is Adidas at risk of bankruptcy? A company goes bankrupt when it can no longer pay its liabilities due with its available assets: the cessation of payments. Solvency is read from the balance sheet, assets by increasing liquidity, liabilities by increasing payability. Beware of liquidity ratios (current, quick, cash ratio): volatile, published too late, and improved by… a WCR increase. Remember the medium-term ratios, among the best predictors of bankruptcy. Stable resources / capital employed: critical point at 70%, Adidas stands at 103%. Net debt / EBITDA: below 3, no problem; above 5, danger; Adidas stands at 1.3. But if Adidas borrows €15bn to buy a competitor, the gauges go haywire. Mind the maturity too: financing a long-lived asset with a short-term loan means gambling with your cash.
toolbox: Short-term ratios (know them to beware of them)

lab.title: The takeover that rattles the gauges
lab.goal: Adidas wants to buy a competitor. Choose the price, the multiple paid, the share financed by debt and its maturity: the net debt / EBITDA, stable resources / capital employed and net debt / CFO gauges turn from green to red live. Find out how far Adidas can borrow, then compare with Europcar.

pdfExample.original: "It's up to you" exercise (assets / liabilities maturity ladder) and the Europcar 2019 exercise: stable resources / capital employed of 59%, net debt / EBITDA of 13.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas's real ratios at 31/12/2025, then a fictitious takeover financed by debt or by a capital increase: how far can Adidas borrow?

valuation.title: Business valuation
valuation.concept: How much is Adidas worth? The stock market gives a price: €169 per share at the end of 2025, i.e. €30bn. But "Price is what you pay; value is what you get." To estimate value, three steps: the market value of the assets (the enterprise value), minus the value of net debt, gives the value of equity. Intrinsic method, the DCF: discount future FCFF at the WACC, then add a Gordon-Shapiro terminal value, FCFF / (WACC − g), which often weighs more than 70% of the total. Two parameters drive everything: the WACC and the perpetual growth g. One point more or less, and the value soars or collapses. Analogical method, multiples: Adidas's EBIT × the EV / EBIT multiple of peers. Quick and "objective", but choosing peers remains… a choice. In practice, combine methods, and stay humble.

lab.title: Adidas mini-DCF: buy, hold or sell?
lab.goal: Set the WACC, the perpetual growth g and growth over the next 5 years: the value per share recalculates against the share price, the curve shows the explosion as g approaches the WACC, the sensitivity matrix gives your analyst verdict. Compare with multiples, then replay the course's Crit exercise.

pdfExample.original: Crit 2021 exercise: FCFF 2022-2026, g = 2%, WACC = 9%, peers at 12 times EBIT; BUY, HOLD or SELL recommendation.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas at 31/12/2025: normative FCFF derived from the 2025 accounts, net debt from the balance sheet, 178.7 million shares and a €169.05 share price. The Crit case can be replayed as is.

derivatives.title: Market finance & derivatives
derivatives.altTitle: Finance de marché et produits dérivés
derivatives.concept: Adidas buys natural rubber in Asia for its soles. If its price soars within six months, the margin melts. On financial markets, a company finds two things: financing (stocks, bonds) and hedges against its risks, derivatives, whose value depends on an underlying asset. With a futures contract, Adidas commits today to buy at a set price: if the price rises, the contract gains what the purchase loses; if it falls, the opposite. The cost is locked in. A firm commitment on both sides, on an organised market with a clearing house and margin calls. With a call option, Adidas pays a premium for the right, not the obligation, to buy at the strike price: protected against a rise, it benefits from a fall. But beware of the Bermuda triangle: reducing market risk exposes you to counterparty and liquidity risks.

lab.title: Hedging simulator: Adidas's rubber
lab.goal: Choose your strategy (no hedge, futures contract or call), then move the rubber price in 6 months: gain or loss on the derivative, net procurement cost and margin calls recalculate, and the payoff profile appears as in the course.

pdfExample.original: A metallurgical company buying a futures contract on 1,000 t of copper at €6,200/t (spot €6,000/t); a Heineken call with a €90 strike for a €5 premium.
pdfExample.adidas: Adidas buys a futures contract on 10,000 t of rubber at €1,550/t (spot €1,500/t): volumes ×10, prices ÷4. The call has the same strike for a premium of €80/t (about 5% of the strike, like the Heineken call).

startup.title: Start-up & restructuring
startup.altTitle: Levée de fonds, faillite et restructuration
startup.concept: Adidas launches Stride Lab, a (fictitious) in-house start-up that 3D-prints soles from recycled plastic. A start-up means extreme risk and negative, random cash flows: no way to pay regular interest. So it is financed with equity, round after round: founders, love money, business angels, then venture capital funds (VC). Classic trap: raising €90m does not give 90% of the power. Investors get INV / POST of the share capital; the rest of their contribution goes to the share premium. Share capital is what splits power. If Stride Lab succeeds: new rounds, an IPO or a sale. If not, and ROCE stays below WACC, it must restructure by raising the economic result. And if cash runs out, it is the cessation of payments, then receivership or liquidation, where shareholders come last.

lab.title: Stride Lab: fundraising… and plan B
lab.goal: Set the pre-money valuation and the amount raised from VCs: the pie chart shows Adidas's dilution, the new balance sheet separates share capital and share premium. Then imagine the worst: if Stride Lab is liquidated, who gets paid back, and in what order?

pdfExample.original: A start-up created with €10k of capital (10 shares of €1,000) raising €90k for a €202.5k post-money value: +€8k of share capital, €82k of share premium, 56% / 44% of the power; order of priority in a judicial liquidation.
pdfExample.adidas: Stride Lab, a fictitious Adidas in-house start-up: €10m of capital (10,000 shares of €1,000), raising €90m for €202.5m post-money. Amounts ×1,000, same percentages.
